statement: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle BAC is 40 degrees. The point D lies on side AC so that BD = BC, as marked. How many degrees is angle ABD?

figure.alt: Triangle ABC with A at the top and base BC, with sides AB and AC the same length. Point D lies on side AC, a little closer to C than to A, and is joined to B. Segments BD and BC each carry two tick marks, showing they are equal. The angle at A is marked 40 degrees.

choices.misconception: I put the two equal angles of triangle BCD at B and D instead of at D and C, so angle DBC came out as 55 degrees and 70 - 55 = 15.
I found angle DBC, 40 degrees, which is the other part of angle ABC, not angle ABD.
I found angle ABC, 70 degrees, the whole angle at B, instead of only the part between BA and BD.
I found angle ADB, 110 degrees, instead of angle ABD.

hints: Look for isosceles triangles in the figure.
Triangle ABC has AB = AC, and triangle BCD has BD = BC. In an isosceles triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides are equal. Start from the 40 degree angle at A.
Angles ABC and ACB are both 70 degrees. In triangle BCD, angle BDC equals angle BCD, so angle DBC = 180 - 70 - 70 = 40.

solutions.reliable: In triangle ABC, AB = AC, so angles ABC and ACB are equal: each is (180 - 40) / 2 = 70 degrees. In triangle BCD, BD = BC, so the angles opposite those sides are equal: angle BDC = angle BCD = 70 degrees. So angle DBC = 180 - 70 - 70 = 40 degrees. Then angle ABD = angle ABC - angle DBC = 70 - 40 = 30 degrees. Check with triangle ABD: angle ADB = 180 - 70 = 110, and 40 + 110 + 30 = 180. The transferable idea: equal sides give equal opposite angles, and a chain of isosceles triangles passes angles from one triangle to the next.
solutions.elegant: Angle BDC = 70 degrees is an outside angle of triangle ABD, so it equals the sum of the two inside angles at A and B: 40 + angle ABD = 70, giving angle ABD = 30.

whyOnTest: Triangle-property questions test spotting isosceles triangles from equal sides and passing angles from one triangle to the next.
